extracted.intended_audience: sports journalists, editors, and readers interested in media ethics and AI in journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Opinion/analysis piece about the ethical, professional, legal and quality implications of using AI to generate sports journalism, and what standards outlets should uphold. Focuses on transparency, quality, accountability, labor effects and representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency / disclose use of A.I.
rubrics_metrics.description: “If you and your business partners are using A.I. writers, just tell us.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should openly disclose when content is generated or substantially produced by AI so readers can decide whether to keep reading. Nondisclosure is framed as unethical and harms trust; disclosure is the minimal expectation. Examples/anti-patterns: hiding AI work behind human bylines (the 'Drew Ortiz' case) is unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest bylines and author attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present AI-generated work as the output of a human author (e.g., creating a fictitious reporter like 'Drew Ortiz' with headshot and bio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bylines should reflect who actually produced the work; fictional or deceptive author personas that mask AI generation are disallowed. Guidance implies either label the piece as AI-generated or use an organizational attribution, and avoid fabricating human identities or bios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and fact-checking responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “How do readers complain when the bots make factual errors? To whom?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when AI produces copy, publishers must ensure mechanisms for fact-checking, corrections and reader complaints. There must be clear editorial responsibility for verifying facts and correcting errors produced by AI; anti-patterns include publishing unvetted AI output without human verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal accountability and liability
rubrics_metrics.description: “And who gets sued if Drew Ortiz defames somebody?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outlets must recognize they (not the AI) bear legal risk for defamation or other harms in AI-generated content. Legal oversight should be applied before publishing AI copy, with clarity on who is responsible and processes to mitigate libel or other legal exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain journalistic quality, insight and original reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: A.I. cannot reproduce the observation, insight or deep reporting of experienced human long-form writers (e.g., Gary Smith-level work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve human reporting for high-value, insight-driven journalism; avoid substituting AI for investigative/long-form pieces that require reporting, nuanced observation and craft. Use human writers/editors where original insight and deep reporting are required. Anti-pattern: relying on AI for the kind of work that produces revealing quotes and long-form narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and labor ethics (compensation effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI replaces paid staff/freelancers (Drew Ortiz's ‘freelance rate — $0.00 per word’), creating a cost/quality and labor-ethical tradeoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and publishers should weigh cost savings against impacts on employment, fair compensation and the sustainability of journalism careers. Ethical practice includes transparency about labor decisions and avoiding deceptive substitution of unpaid AI content for paid human work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic diversity and representation (avoid tokenism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using AI-generated headshots/names to signal multiculturalism (e.g., 'He might look white, but his last name is Ortiz. Drew is our highest-profile Hispanic staffer.') is misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outlets should not manufacture appearances of diversity via fabricated AI personas. Authentic hiring and representation are required; using AI to feign diversity is unethical and undermines genuine inclusion efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human editorial oversight / human-in-the-loop
rubrics_metrics.description: AI-generated copy needs human supervision, editing and judgment rather than being published verbatim as autonomous journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement processes where humans review, correct, contextualize and add reporting value to AI drafts. Maintain editors who can judge nuance, context, ethics and legal risk. Anti-pattern: treating AI as a fully independent journalist needing no oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of feedback loops and provenance ('robots teaching robots')
rubrics_metrics.description: “A.I. writing learns from what's already published, and if more of it floods the internet we'll have robots teaching robots.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about widespread AI content that trains future models on lower-quality AI-generated text, producing degradation of quality over time. Consider provenance, training data sources, and limits on uncurated AI-generated publishing to avoid escalating quality decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer recourse and complaint channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers need ways to complain and obtain corrections when AI makes errors; otherwise accountability is unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should maintain clear, accessible processes for readers to report errors in AI-written pieces, with visible correction policies and responsible contacts. Anti-patterns include opaque processes that leave readers with no practical remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical defensibility of passing off AI as human
rubrics_metrics.description: “Passing off A.I.-generated content as the work of humans is ethically indefensible and practically untenable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit normative standard: do not misrepresent AI work as human-authored. Ethical policy should forbid deception and require labeling/attribution; consider reputational and trust harms when deciding editorial policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial/product investment versus short-term cost-cutting
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers will lean toward the cheapest options until consumer backlash prompts them to invest in the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-makers should balance short-term cost savings from AI against long-term product quality, brand trust and audience expectations. Strategy should include readiness to invest in journalistic quality if audience response demands it; avoid reflexive substitution of AI to cut costs without regard for product value.
